figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Illustration of generative paradigms for inverse problems. (a) and (b) depict trajectory-space methods, while panels (c) and (d) depict source-space optimization methods. (a) Likelihood score corrections are applied directly at each noisy intermediate state $\mathbf{x}_{t}$. (b) Likelihood score corrections are applied in clean image space via the Tweedie estimate $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{0|t}$, followed by renoising to the generative manifold at the next timestep. (c) Source-space MAP methods reparameterize the clean image via the deterministic generative map $\Phi$ as $\mathbf{x}_{0}=\Phi(\mathbf{x}_{1})$ and optimize over the initial noise $\mathbf{x}_{1}$ to minimize data fidelity. (d) Source-space posterior sampling draws samples from $p(\mathbf{x}_{1}\mid\mathbf{y})$ via Hamiltonian Monte Carlo or Langevin dynamics. (e) By strategically coupling proximal source initialization with bounded stochasticity during guided posterior sampling, FLINT bounds the sampling trajectory, preserving the initialization advantage and yielding high-fidelity convergence.
figures.headline: Schematic contrasts trajectory-space and source-space methods with FLINT, which couples proximal initialization with bounded stochasticity.
citing_sentences: 1(a) and (b)).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Interplay of proximal initialization and sampling stochasticity on Gaussian deblurring. (a) PSNR and LPIPS as functions of the perturbation scale $C_{0}$ across varying the cumulative stochasticity $G$, demonstrating the existence of a sufficiency regime ($C_{0}\leq 0.4$ in this setup) where proximal initialization performs on par with exact inversion. (b) Visual comparisons for $C_{0}\in\{0,0.4,\pi/2\}$. While a representative proximal initialization within this regime ($C_{0}=0.4$) matches the high fidelity of exact inversion under posterior sampling ($G=0.008$), it preserves measurement-consistent structures even in unconditional sampling, unlike the unrelated output from random initialization.
figures.headline: Proximal initialization matches exact inversion up to perturbation scale 0.4, and quality falls as cumulative stochasticity rises.
citing_sentences: Figure 2(a) visualizes the perception-distortion landscape as a joint function of the perturbation scale $C_{0}$, reflecting $\delta^{2}$ along the horizontal axis, and the cumulative stochasticity $G$ across the curve family.
Across all $G$ curves in Figure 2(a), reconstruction quality remains nearly flat within an initial proximity range before it begins to degrade.
Figure 2(b) qualitatively corroborates this.

figures.label: Figure S11
figures.caption: Qualitative failure cases of FLINT on highly complex scenes (DIV2K dataset). Increased ill-posedness in dense, multi-object images disrupts the balance between measurement fidelity and the generative prior. This results in either hallucinated structures, where the model generates spurious details to satisfy the prior, or blurry textures, where conflicting updates fail to resolve high-frequency information. These cases highlight the inherited limitations of the pretrained backbone’s capacity for complex out-of-distribution scenes.
figures.headline: Failure cases on dense multi-object DIV2K scenes show hallucinated structures or blurry textures.

abstract: Flow matching models have emerged as a dominant paradigm for generative posterior sampling in imaging inverse problems. Existing solvers follow two distinct lines of work: trajectory-space methods, which refine sampling dynamics from random initial noise, and source-space methods, which optimize the initial noise itself. While most prior work treats these as independent design choices, we show that they are inherently coupled. We derive a unified stability bound that links initialization proximity and cumulative sampling stochasticity through a multiplicative envelope, complemented by two empirical observations. First, we identify a sufficiency regime in which a moderately optimized proximal source initialization is enough to attain the performance plateau, rendering exhaustive source-space optimization unnecessary. Second, this initial advantage is fragile: it is eroded by excessive stochasticity accumulation during guided sampling, necessitating a mechanism that bounds the cumulative noise injection. These findings motivate FLINT, a two-stage framework that operationalizes this coupling. FLINT establishes a high-fidelity starting point via a manifold-constrained proximal objective in only a few iterations, then performs guided sampling under a bounded stochasticity schedule that helps prevent erasure of the initialization advantage. Across diverse inverse problems, FLINT delivers state of the art perceptual quality and competitive distortion metrics while maintaining superior computational efficiency.

sections.body: Flow matching models serve as priors for imaging inverse problems. Trajectory-space methods refine sampling from random initial noise, and source-space methods optimize that noise. The paper argues the two design choices are coupled rather than independent. It derives a stability bound linking initialization proximity and cumulative sampling stochasticity, reports two empirical observations, and proposes FLINT. FLINT runs a few manifold-constrained proximal iterations for initialization, then performs guided sampling under a bounded stochasticity schedule. The paper evaluates on diverse inverse problems.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing posterior samplers either fix the starting noise or optimize it alone; FLINT couples both choices.

sections.body: Rectified flow defines a velocity network and a flow-based Tweedie estimate of the clean image from any intermediate state. Posterior solvers split into trajectory-space methods, which steer intermediate states, and source-space methods, which optimize the initial noise through the deterministic generative map. Source-space optimization is costly because it requires backpropagation through the full N-step reverse ODE. Two reductions are used. Truncated sampling integrates only the first K-1 steps before applying Tweedie's formula. The Shortcut Diffusion Optimization approximation keeps the computational graph only at the first denoising step. The paper combines both reductions in its method.
sections.heading: Background
sections.headline: Background defines flow-based posterior sampling and the truncated, shortcut-based gradients that make source optimization cheaper.

sections.body: The section analyzes a reverse-time posterior flow SDE and states Proposition 3.1. It bounds the expected squared terminal deviation from a reference trajectory by a prefactor times the sum of a squared initialization error and d times G, where G is cumulative stochasticity. Two consequences follow. When the initialization error term is much smaller than d times G, further reducing initialization error has little effect. Increasing G raises the bound regardless of initialization. On Gaussian deblurring with FlowDPS over 100 FFHQ samples, reconstruction quality stays nearly flat up to a perturbation scale of 0.4, which the paper calls the sufficiency regime, and degrades as G increases. The authors state the bound does not establish convergence to the exact posterior.
sections.heading: Analysis: Coupling of Proximal Initialization and Sampling Stochasticity
sections.headline: The stability bound predicts a sufficiency regime and erosion by stochasticity, and Gaussian deblurring experiments are consistent with both.

sections.body: Stage 1 minimizes a Kullback-Leibler (KL) objective over a Gaussian surrogate on the initial noise. It combines a data-fidelity term, a prior term, and a higher-order cumulant regularizer, and is optimized for a few iterations with a single-sample estimator. Spectrally weighted data consistency multiplies the measurement gradient by a Wiener-style filter that down-weights high frequencies, which the truncated estimate resolves poorly. Stage 2 starts from the Stage 1 output and runs guided sampling. At each step it applies data consistency to the clean estimate and renoises the result. The stochasticity schedule is `eta(t)` equal to `lambda_s` times the square root of one minus `sigma_t`, times `sigma_t`, which is near zero at both ends of the trajectory. The paper states that `lambda_s` below 1 keeps the integral of `eta(t)` squared bounded.
sections.heading: Method: The FLINT Framework
sections.headline: FLINT runs a few proximal optimization steps for initialization, then guided sampling under a bell-shaped stochasticity schedule.

sections.body: Experiments use FFHQ (1k samples) and DIV2K (800 samples) on Stable Diffusion 3.5-Medium with a 50 NFE budget, where NFE means network function evaluations. FLINT splits this into 21 NFEs for Stage 1 and 29 for Stage 2. Table 1 reports that FLINT outperforms all flow matching baselines on distortion and perceptual metrics. On Stable Diffusion 1.5 with 200 NFEs, FLINT gives the best PSNR, FID, and LPIPS on super-resolution ×4 and motion deblurring. In Gaussian deblurring ablations, PSNR rises from 28.56 with random initialization to 30.11 with full Stage 1. The bell-shaped schedule at `lambda_s` 0.8 gives 30.11 PSNR, while 1.3 gives 29.88 and 0.3 gives 29.59.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: FLINT outperforms flow matching baselines, and ablations show that proximal initialization and the bell-shaped schedule both contribute.

sections.body: The conclusion restates FLINT as a two-stage framework that couples proximal source initialization with bounded stochasticity. It claims consistent reconstruction gains at a competitive sampling cost. The limitation paragraph states that FLINT inherits the limitations of its pretrained generative models, including training data biases and reduced capacity for out-of-distribution images. It also states that reconstruction quality may degrade on scenes with high structural complexity, such as multiple objects or instances, because increased ill-posedness makes it hard to satisfy data fidelity and prior consistency at once.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The conclusion restates the coupling principle, and the limitations are inherited prior biases and weaker results on complex scenes.

sections.body: The appendix gives proofs of the posterior energy bound and of Proposition 3.1. It reports an ablation of the cumulant regularizer on Motion Deblurring, with PSNR 30.32 when off and 30.39 when on. Table S7 compares FLINT with forward-noising, deterministic-inversion, and stochastic-inversion initializations, and FLINT attains the best score on every metric. An excessive-optimization study finds PSNR gains of 0.36 dB from step 10 to 40, while LPIPS rises from 0.202 to 0.274, an increase of over 35%. A posterior variance analysis reports meaningful pixel-wise spread in high-frequency regions. The appendix ends with additional qualitative comparisons and failure cases.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists energy-bound proofs, cumulant and initialization comparisons, excessive optimization, posterior variance, and extra qualitative results.
